title: Solve it together: double, then is it big?
idea: GUIDED (UEPCC). Compose a transforming helper with a testing helper: double a number, then ask if the result is big.
problem: double(n) returns n*2 and is_big(n) returns n > 10. Show is_big(double(6)).

exercises.prompt:
PROBLEM: double(n) returns n*2; is_big(n) returns n > 10. Show is_big(double(6)).

What is the OUTPUT?
options: True or False — whether 6 doubled is greater than 10
exercises.explanation: Output is a True/False. We double first, then test if that result is big. Name the output first.

exercises.prompt: Which runs first — the transform or the test?
options: The transform (double) runs first, then its result is tested
exercises.explanation: Inner call first: double(6) becomes 12, then is_big(12) tests it. Inside-out.

exercises.prompt: Example by hand. Double 6 is 12; is 12 greater than 10?
exercises.explanation: 12 > 10 is True. Hand-work it so Check has a known answer.

exercises.prompt: A helper can return a True/False that another part of the code then uses.
exercises.explanation: Yes. is_big returns a boolean. Composing a transform with a test is a common, useful pattern.

blocks: Test whether that result is big
exercises.explanation: Transform first, then test, then show. The inner result feeds the outer test.

exercises.prompt: In is_big(double(6)), what value does is_big actually receive?
exercises.explanation: double(6) returns 12, so is_big receives 12. The returned value becomes the argument.

exercises.prompt: Code it: define double, define is_big, then compose in a print.
exercises.explanation: Define both helpers, then feed double(6) into is_big. double(6)=12, is_big(12)=True.

exercises.prompt:
Compose so double runs first, then the test:

print(is_big(____(6)))
exercises.explanation: double(6) is the inner call (12); is_big(12) is True.

exercises.prompt: Check — the code prints True; your example said True. So...
exercises.explanation: Output (True) matches the hand-worked True. The composition is correct.
double(3)=6, and 6 > 10 is False. Works for new inputs — the solution generalizes.
